claim: L1's mechanical `conditioned_scope_clause.is_unconditioned_subject` flag only inspects the text preceding the requirement's first RFC2119 keyword (the subject clause). It does NOT detect applicability-narrowing restrictions embedded later in the sentence, inside the verb phrase or object -- e.g. req-1-eip155-chainid's subject is bare 'Tested code' (flagged unconditioned=True), but the actual obligation is 'create hashes FOR TRANSACTIONS that incorporate chainid' -- 'for transactions' is a real restriction (this only applies to code that constructs off-chain-signable transaction-style hashes, e.g. EIP-712/meta-tx/permit signatures; a contract that never does this is NOT_APPLICABLE), just not captured by the mechanical subject-clause flag. Similarly req-2-overflow-underflow's bare 'Tested code' subject hides the real restriction 'contain calculations that CAN overflow or underflow' -- applicability requires arithmetic operations capable of overflow/underflow (largely relevant only to pre-0.8.0 code, `unchecked{}` blocks, or inline-assembly arithmetic, given Solidity >=0.8.0's default overflow checks), not literally all code.
why_unavoidable: Reliably distinguishing 'restriction in the subject clause' from 'restriction in the predicate/object' via pure regex/HTML-structure parsing (L1's approach) would require a much deeper syntactic (near-NLP) parse than the mechanical, auditable extraction the L1 parser is designed to do. Rather than build that speculative NLP layer now, this is logged as a required MANUAL RE-READ step at L3 for every requirement, not solved mechanically.
blast_radius: any future Track B requirement whose is_unconditioned_subject=True must be manually re-read for predicate-embedded restrictions before its L3 applicability_rule is trusted

claim: The L6 trigger component description for req-2-verify-exact-balance-check ('trigger-exact-balance-eq') extends the detectable pattern to 'an `==`/`!=` comparison where one operand is ... a call to a balanceOf-shaped function' -- but the requirement's own text says only 'the balance of an account', which directly and unambiguously names native ETH balance (Solidity's `.balance` member, matching the sibling S requirement req-1-exact-balance-check's own wording). Generalizing to ERC20-style `balanceOf()` token balances is importing an external Solidity/token-standard convention not stated in EthTrust's text -- caught during a self-review pass for this go/no-go check, not by the original L6 authoring.
why_unavoidable: Not unavoidable -- this is a correctable overreach, not a genuine textual gap. Logged here rather than silently narrowed, per the register's purpose of surfacing exactly this kind of creeping generalization before it goes unnoticed into Track B.
resolution: Corrected in the same pass: trigger-exact-balance-eq's note narrowed to '.balance'-style native-ETH comparisons only, matching req-1-exact-balance-check's own wording. No textual basis for including token balanceOf() was found elsewhere in the spec.

claim: The independent-reviewer subagent classified pooltogether/H-02 (a uint256-to-uint96 narrowing downcast in Vault._burn that silently truncates share amounts) as DIRECT evidence for req-2-overflow-underflow ('calculations that can overflow or underflow'). Verified against the actual finding text (confirmed fix: 'Added SafeCast') and found this conflates two distinct failure classes: a narrowing TYPE CAST that truncates a value (no arithmetic operation involved, nothing 'calculates' anything) versus an arithmetic CALCULATION whose result exceeds/goes below its type's representable range. Corrected to CONTEXTUAL in rtf/l11_correspondence/correspondence_mapping.json.
why_unavoidable: Not unavoidable -- corrected on manual verification. Logged because this is exactly the kind of plausible-sounding-but-technically-wrong conflation an independent reviewer (human or model) can make when working at speed across many findings, and because 9 of the same reviewer's other 9 req-2-overflow-underflow classifications were checked and found genuinely well-grounded (real arithmetic operations, real underflow/overflow mechanisms cited with specific code) -- this was not a systemic failure of the correspondence-building process, but it does mean 'independent review' alone, without a verification pass by whoever consumes the mapping, is not sufficient quality assurance on its own.
blast_radius: any future L12 evaluation using this correspondence mapping for recall metrics -- the DIRECT-mapping count for req-2-overflow-underflow drops from 10 to 9 as a result
resolution: Corrected in place in correspondence_mapping.json; review_status field on that record updated to 'corrected_on_manual_verification_by_orchestrating_session' rather than silently overwritten with no trace.

req_id_or_section: multiple req-3-implement-as-documented correspondence records (e.g. 2024-04-noya/H-13, H-14, H-22; 2024-04-noya/H-09, H-11)
claim: Several req-3-implement-as-documented correspondence records cite documentation of a THIRD-PARTY protocol the audited code integrates with (Balancer, Synthetix, Pendle) rather than the audited project's OWN documentation (which is what req-3-documented/req-3-document-system, and by extension req-3-implement-as-documented, literally reference). Whether 'the audited code misuses a third-party protocol's documented API' counts as this Tested Code failing to 'behave as described in the documentation provided for [Document Contract Logic]/[Document System Architecture]' is a genuine scope question, not resolved here either way -- a defensible reading exists on both sides (the project's own documentation of its integration behavior implicitly commits to correct usage, versus: only the project's own explicit claims count, and misusing an external API is an integration-correctness bug, not a documentation-conformance bug).
why_unavoidable: This is a real interpretive ambiguity in how far req-3-implement-as-documented's scope extends, not a derivation error -- flagged for expert review (per the L10 maturity model) rather than resolved unilaterally by either the independent reviewer or this correction pass.
blast_radius: An unknown subset of the 40 req-3-implement-as-documented records in rtf/l11_correspondence/correspondence_mapping.json -- not narrowed or removed, since the scope question is unresolved, not decided against them

req_id_or_section: L1 corpus-wide parser (surfaced via req-2-documented, req-2-self-destruct, req-2-external-calls, req-2-check-rounding, req-2-safe-assembly, req-2-protect-create2, req-2-malleable-signatures-for-replay -- 7 requirements found during Track B M-level work)
claim: L1's `extend_until_modality` sibling-block-gluing logic only activates when the header paragraph has NO RFC2119 keyword at all. Several requirements have their RFC2119 keyword INSIDE the header (e.g. 'Tested Code MUST document the need for each instance of:'), immediately followed by a colon introducing a <ul> that is essential to the requirement's actual content (in req-2-documented's case, 8 specifically named trigger constructs) -- but because a MUST is already found in the header, the gluing rule never fires, so `normative_text` silently truncates at the colon, and this truncation propagates into every L2 context bundle's `self` field (which reads directly from `normative_text`). Not caught during Phase 0/1 development because none of the 6 Track A requirements happened to have this shape; found only once Track B's broader M-level sweep hit real examples.
why_unavoidable: Not unavoidable -- a real, fixable parser gap (the same fix pattern already built for the no-keyword-at-all case generalizes: also glue a following <ul> when the header ends in ':' regardless of whether a keyword was already found). Not yet fixed in rtf/l1_corpus/parse_spec.py as of this entry -- the 7 affected requirements' true full text was extracted by hand (direct raw HTML read) for this Track B M-level analysis pass, bypassing the truncated L1/L2 fields for just these 7, rather than blocking on a parser fix mid-batch.
blast_radius: rtf/l1_corpus/requirement_corpus.json's normative_text field for these 7 requirements (and any others sharing this colon-terminated-header shape not yet enumerated -- a full corpus sweep for this pattern has not been done)
rtf/l2_context_bundles/*.json's 'self' field for the same 7+ requirements, since it reads normative_text directly
any future L3+ work on these requirements MUST re-verify against raw HTML rather than trusting the L1/L2 fields at face value until the parser is fixed and re-run
resolution: Fixed in rtf/l1_corpus/parse_spec.py (_looks_incomplete() generalizes the extension trigger to colon-terminated headers and dangling-keyword cases), full corpus re-parsed and L2 bundles regenerated. Diff against the pre-fix corpus confirmed 7 requirements changed (all pure extensions, zero shortened), referential integrity held before and after. See PARSING_NOTES.md for the full writeup.

claim: The framework's PASS/FAIL/INCONCLUSIVE/INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE conformance schema (L8) was designed with MUST-level requirements in mind. 10 of 11 GP requirements use SHOULD, an explicitly non-binding, non-certification-blocking recommendation per RFC2119 convention and per EthTrust's own certification model (Level [S]/[M]/[Q] gates are built from MUST requirements; GP is a separate, advisory section). Whether a 'FAIL' on a SHOULD-level requirement should be reported identically to a 'FAIL' on a MUST-level one (same schema, same downstream metrics) or whether GP results need a distinguishable presentation (e.g. an 'ADVISORY_NOT_MET' state, or simply excluding GP from any pass/fail-rate metric entirely) was not resolved in this pass -- generated GP records using the same PASS/FAIL vocabulary as MUST-level requirements for consistency, but flagging this as a genuine, not-yet-decided design question rather than a silent choice.
why_unavoidable: A real open design question, not an error -- reusing the existing schema was the pragmatic choice to keep GP records in the same shape as the rest of the corpus for this pass, but the underlying question (does non-binding advisory conformance deserve a different formal state than binding conformance) deserves a real decision before any GP results are reported in evaluation metrics.
blast_radius: Any future L12 evaluation that includes GP requirements in aggregate pass/fail statistics without separating them from MUST-level results
rtf/track_a/l_gp_recommended_practice/*.json's use of the standard PASS/FAIL vocabulary

claim: find_create2_usage()'s assembly-shape branch (committed in an earlier L5 pass) checked `node.inline_asm` for the literal 'create2' substring on ASSEMBLY-type nodes. Direct inspection during req-2-protect-create2 implementation found that Slither's `node.inline_asm` (backed by `_asm_source_code`) is NOT populated for a stock 0.8.20 compile of a plain `assembly { ... }` block -- it returns None even when the block plainly contains `create2` -- so this branch was silently dead code: it could never fire, regardless of input. Not caught earlier because the original test_predicates.py::test_create2 only exercised the high-level `new X{salt:...}()` shape, never the assembly shape, so the always-None condition never surfaced as a test failure.
why_unavoidable: Not unavoidable -- a real, fixable predicate bug, found only because implementing req-2-protect-create2's own assembly-create2 evidence-gap case required exercising this code path with a real fixture for the first time.
blast_radius: find_create2_usage()'s assembly-detection branch for req-1-no-create2 -- any prior claim that this requirement's assembly-CREATE2 shape was covered was incorrect; only the high-level new{salt:} shape was ever actually detected

the new find_create2_deployed_target_violations() for req-2-protect-create2, which shares the same node-text-extraction technique and would have inherited the identical dead-code bug had it not been caught here first
resolution: Added `_assembly_block_text(node)` helper in rtf/l5_predicates/predicates.py, falling back to `node.source_mapping.content` (confirmed reliably populated) when `node.inline_asm` is empty. Both find_create2_usage() and find_create2_deployed_target_violations() switched to this helper. New test coverage added for the previously-untested assembly-create2 shape in both test_create2() and test_create2_deployed_target_violations(); full suite (67/67) passing after the fix.

claim: Slither exposes no variable-read/write IR at all for identifiers referenced only inside an `assembly {}` block (confirmed empirically: `node.variables_written`/`node.state_variables_written` are always empty for ASSEMBLY-type nodes, even for a simple `sstore(fp.slot, raw)` case), so req-2-safe-assembly's predicate is necessarily built as a text-level regex match against the assembly block's raw source (via `_assembly_block_text`), not an IR-level one -- a real, load-bearing tool limitation, not a design choice. Separately and more severely: Slither's own Yul parser (`slither/solc_parsing/yul/parse_yul.py`) CRASHES with `SlitherException: unresolved reference to identifier <x>.address` when analyzing `.selector`/`.address` assignment on a LOCAL variable of EXTERNAL function-pointer type inside assembly -- confirmed by direct compilation attempt. This is Solidity's own supported syntax for that variable shape (the compiler itself rejects `.slot` there, only `.selector`/`.address` are valid) -- so this specific sub-case of req-2-safe-assembly's 'arbitrary values ... assigned to variables of type function' clause cannot be analyzed by Slither AT ALL, not even to the point of producing a compiled Slither object to run a predicate against.
why_unavoidable: A genuine upstream tool limitation (Slither's Yul parser does not support this valid Solidity construct), not a predicate design gap -- no predicate, however written, can run against a compilation that Slither itself cannot complete.
blast_radius: find_unsafe_assembly_variable_write()'s coverage of req-2-safe-assembly's function-typed-variable attack surface is necessarily partial: covers state-variable .slot-based writes (via sstore/`.slot :=`) but structurally cannot cover local external-function-pointer .selector/.address assignment

any future Level-S/M predicate touching assembly-block variable access inherits the same 'no variable IR inside assembly' limitation and must use the same text-level fallback, not assume Slither IR is available

req_id_or_section: L12 execution orchestrator (all requirements evaluated against real, multi-file EVMbench targets)
claim: Foundry (`forge`) cannot be installed on this HPC node -- confirmed via a real `foundryup` install attempt, not assumed: the precompiled binaries require GLIBC >= 2.29, and this node's glibc is older (foundryup itself reported 'GLIBC_2.29 not found' for forge/cast/anvil/chisel). Slither's own crytic-compile, when the compilation target lives inside a directory tree containing a `foundry.toml` (true for essentially every real EVMbench audit target, since EVMbench's own audits are Foundry projects), unconditionally shells out to `forge config`/`forge build` for two SEPARATE reasons discovered by direct trial: (1) `_init_platform`'s own Foundry detection when no `compile_force_framework` override is given, AND (2) even WITH `compile_force_framework='solc'` correctly forcing the actual compile platform, crytic_compile.py's `__init__` still runs a SEPARATE 'try to auto-detect remappings/solc-version from the working directory's build framework' check whenever the CWD (not just the target) is inside a Foundry project -- this second check is NOT gated by `compile_force_framework` at all.
why_unavoidable: The GLIBC mismatch is a genuine, unavoidable environment constraint on this specific node -- not fixable without root/a newer OS image. The crytic-compile auto-detection behavior is real upstream tool behavior (confirmed by reading crytic_compile.py's source directly, not guessed), not a bug in this project's own code.
blast_radius: Any L12 orchestrator run against a real, multi-file EVMbench target (as opposed to this project's single-file synthetic test fixtures) needs the workaround in rtf/l5_predicates/compile_helper.py::compile_evmbench_target() -- setting cwd to a directory with no reachable foundry.toml, and supplying every import remapping (collected recursively across ALL nested lib/ dependencies' own remappings.txt files, not just the project's top-level one) as absolute paths explicitly, rather than relying on crytic-compile's normal Foundry-aware auto-configuration
resolution: Implemented rtf/l5_predicates/compile_helper.py::compile_evmbench_target() (+ _collect_remappings()), confirmed working end-to-end against the real 2023-07-pooltogether Vault.sol (36 real contracts compiled, including Vault, PrizePool, TwabController, and their full real dependency graph -- OpenZeppelin, prb-math, etc.), with zero forge invocation. One unrelated, separately-logged Slither IR-generation limitation surfaced on TierCalculationLib.getTierOdds during this same compile (a 'NoneType has no attribute parameters' internal error) -- a genuine Slither limitation on this specific function, not connected to the remapping/cwd workaround itself, and does not block compilation of the rest of the target.

claim: The first implementation of target_localization_accuracy() compared only the CONTRACT NAME prefix of a location string ('Vault' from 'Vault._burn'), not the full 'Contract.function' location -- a real bug, not caught by this module's own unit tests at the time, because the existing negative-case test happened to use a DIFFERENT contract name (masking the same-contract-different-function false-positive case entirely). Found by this project's own FIRST real evaluation run against 2023-07-pooltogether: it reported 2/2 (100%) target localization accuracy, but manual inspection of the raw evidence showed the H-02 finding's real ground-truth locations (Vault._mint/_burn/_transfer, extracted directly from the fix-patch diff) were never actually present in RTF's collected evidence for that requirement (find_unvalidated_function_parameters only scans public/external functions; _mint/_burn/_transfer are internal overrides) -- the metric was trivially matching on the shared contract name alone.
why_unavoidable: A genuine implementation defect in the metrics module itself, not a design tradeoff -- caught only by actually running a real evaluation against real ground truth with real (not synthetic) location data, exactly the kind of gap synthetic unit tests alone could not have revealed.
blast_radius: Any metric result computed with the pre-fix target_localization_accuracy() would have overstated localization precision for any target where multiple candidate locations share one contract/file -- true of essentially every real Solidity file with more than one function

The first frozen evaluation's manifest (frozen at git commit d4f7ba6) is stale relative to this fix and was re-frozen after -- see freeze_gate.py's refusal to silently overwrite a frozen manifest, which correctly required an explicit delete+re-freeze step for this fix
resolution: Fixed to compare the full lowercased location string (Contract.function), not just the contract-name prefix. New regression test added (test_target_localization_accuracy's same-contract-different-function case) specifically covering the shape of bug that let this through originally. Permitted post-evaluation change reason per the plan's policy: 'implementation defect' -- re-computed, not tuned to any observed benchmark score (the fix makes the metric MORE conservative/harsher, not more favorable).
